components.note: 廴 (to move forward, extend) — 建 relates to constructing or setting something up over an extended process.
聿 (yù) gives a hint of the sound — 建 is pronounced jiàn, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
讠 (speech) — relates to 议's meaning 'to discuss, deliberate; opinion.'
义 (yì) gives the sound — 议 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiànyì nǐ zǎodiǎn xiūxi.
example.english: I suggest you rest earlier.
example.fact: 建议 works as both a verb (“to suggest”) and a noun (“a suggestion”) with no change in form — 提出建议 (“to put forward a suggestion”) and 我建议 (“I suggest”) both use the same two characters, one of many Chinese words that cross the verb/noun line freely.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 做 relates to a person carrying out an action.
故 (cause, reason, to happen) — combined with 亻 (person), 做 came to mean 'to make' or 'to do,' someone actively causing something to happen.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我一定会做到我的承诺。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yídìng huì zuòdào wǒ de chéngnuò.
example.english: I will definitely fulfill my promise.
example.fact: 做到 is a verb plus a result complement: 做 (“to do”) plus 到 (“to arrive, reach”) — 到 here doesn't mean physical arrival but marks that the action of 做 actually succeeded, the same “verb + 到 = success” pattern behind 看到 (“to see, to succeed in seeing”) and 听到 (“to hear, to succeed in hearing”).

components.note: 尸 (body) — 屁 relates to a bodily function.
比 (bǐ) gives a sound only distantly related to pì today, having drifted apart over time.
⺼ (flesh/body) — 股 originally referred to the thigh, a part of the body
殳 (shū) gives a sound related to 股's reading gǔ, though the two have drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 小孩子摔了一下,屁股很疼。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo háizi shuāi le yíxià, pìgu hěn téng.
example.english: The little kid fell, and their bottom really hurts.
example.fact: 屁股 sits at a casual, everyday register — fine in ordinary conversation the way English “butt” is, but not the word a doctor or formal document would reach for, which would use a more clinical term instead.

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
日 depicts the sun as a circle with a dot or short stroke inside — a simplified picture of the sun's disc, later squared off in the standard script.

example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ shēngrì kuàilè!
example.english: Happy birthday to you!
example.fact: 生日 is the plain, everyday word for “birthday” (生 “to be born” + 日 “day”) — for a revered figure's birthday, especially a historical or religious one (as in 孔子诞辰, “Confucius's birthday”), Chinese instead reaches for the more formal and reverent 诞辰, a register distinction with no single English equivalent.

components.note: 日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'
宀 (a roof, house) — 安 pictures shelter.
女 (woman) — a woman safely inside a house gave 安 its meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'

example.pinyin: “Wǎn'ān, zuò gè hǎomèng.” “Wǎn'ān!”
example.english: “Good night, sweet dreams.” “Good night!”
example.fact: 晚安 works only as a parting word said right before sleep — for an evening greeting said upon arrival, Chinese uses 晚上好 instead, splitting a job that English “good evening” and “good night” also split, but along a slightly different line.

components.note: 不 (not) — 否 relates directly to negation and denial
口 (kǒu) gives a loose sound connection to 否's reading fǒu
贝 (a shell, an ancient form of currency/valuables) — represents the property or standards that rules protect.
刂 (a knife) — depicts laws being carved or inscribed onto a slate, the source of 则's meaning 'rule, standard.'

example.hanzi: 你要快点,否则就迟到了。
example.pinyin: Nǐ yào kuàidiǎn, fǒuzé jiù chídào le.
example.english: You need to hurry, otherwise you'll be late.
example.fact: 否则 almost always sets up a clause that follows with 就 (“否则就...”), the same way 如果 pairs with 就 — 就 marks the natural, almost automatic consequence of whatever comes before it.

components.note: 宀 (a roof, house) — 安 pictures shelter.
女 (woman) — a woman safely inside a house gave 安 its meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'
扌 (hand) — 排 relates to arranging things by hand into order
非 (fēi) gives a sound distantly related to 排's reading pái, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Zhècì lǚxíng shì shéi ānpái de?
example.english: Who arranged this trip?
example.fact: 安排 crosses freely between verb (“to arrange”) and noun (“an arrangement, a plan”) — 工作安排 (“work arrangements”) needs no different word than 我安排了这次旅行 (“I arranged this trip”).

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'
车 (cart) — 轻 originally described a light, nimble cart, extended to 'light (weight), gentle.'
工 (gōng) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from qīng.

example.pinyin: Tā kàn qǐlai hěn niánqīng.
example.english: He looks very young.
example.fact: 轻 on its own means “light” in weight, as its own etymology (a light, nimble cart) shows — 年轻 borrows that sense of lightness metaphorically for a person's age, pairing 年 (“years”) with an image of being unburdened by age, not unlike English describing someone as having a “youthful lightness.”

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.
面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng kàn xiàmiàn de lìzi.
example.english: Please look at the example below.
example.fact: Beyond its literal spatial sense “below,” 下面 is a common discourse marker for “next” in speech and writing (下面我们介绍..., “next, we will introduce...”) — a physical direction word repurposed as a tool for organizing what comes next in a talk or text.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姑 names a female relative.
古 (old) — combined with woman, originally suggesting an older female relative, an aunt, giving 姑 its meaning.
女 (woman) — 娘 names a female relative, mother or young woman.
良 (liáng) gives a sound close to niáng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 那个姑娘唱歌唱得真好。
example.pinyin: Nàge gūniang chàng gē chàng de zhēn hǎo.
example.english: That girl sings really well.
example.fact: 姑娘 carries a warmer, slightly old-fashioned or rural flavor next to the plainer, more modern 女孩 — a register difference worth noticing before picking between the two, not unlike English “lass” sitting beside plain “girl.”

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钥 names an object made of metal.
月 (yuè) gives a sound distantly related to yào, having drifted apart over time.
匕 (a blade-like shape, used for spoon-like utensils) — 匙 named a spoon.
是 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with the "shi" reading of 匙.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ yàoshi wàng zài jiā lǐ le.
example.english: I forgot my keys at home.
example.fact: 钥匙 pairs 钥 (a metal-radical character tied to locks) with 匙, the same character that independently means “spoon” (as in 汤匙, “soup spoon”) — a widely repeated, if hard to fully verify, explanation traces this to older keys having a long, thin, spoon-like shape.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 法官宣布了最终的判决。
example.pinyin: Fǎguān xuānbù le zuìzhōng de pànjué.
example.english: The judge announced the final verdict.
example.fact: 法官 literally combines 法 (“law”) with 官 (“official”) — “law official” — the same building pattern behind other government-role words like 警官 (“police officer”) and 长官 (“commanding officer”).

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — 选 relates to the process of selecting, as if moving through options
先 (xiān) gives a sound close to 选's reading xuǎn
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.hanzi: 每个国家都派出了自己的选手。
example.pinyin: Měi gè guójiā dōu pàichū le zìjǐ de xuǎnshǒu.
example.english: Every country sent its own athletes.
example.fact: 选手 literally “selected hand” (选 “to select” + 手, here meaning “a person skilled at something,” as in 高手 “expert”) — the word specifically implies someone chosen through competition, not just any participant or player.

components.note: 自 (nose) — the breath passing through.
心 (heart) — the breath of life, giving 息 its meaning 'to breathe; to rest; news.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng tígōng gèng duō de xìnxī.
example.english: Please provide more information.
example.fact: 信息 already meant “news, information” well before the computer age, but it's now closely tied to computing-era terms like 信息技术 (“information technology”) — pairing 信 (“letter, trust”) with 息 (“breath, news”), an old vocabulary combination that just happened to fit a 20th-century concept perfectly.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 投 relates to throwing something with the hand
殳 (shū) gives a loose sound connection to 投's reading tóu
覀 here depicts rising flames.
示 (altar) — burning paper offerings over an altar, a traditional practice, gave 票 its meaning of a paper note, later 'ticket, banknote.'

example.hanzi: 我们下周要投票选新班长。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xià zhōu yào tóupiào xuǎn xīn bānzhǎng.
example.english: We're going to vote for a new class monitor next week.
example.fact: 投票 literally means “to throw a ticket” (投 “to throw, cast” + 票 “ticket, note”) — the same 投 that shows up in 投篮 (“to shoot a basketball”) and 投递 (“to deliver mail”), all sharing the sense of propelling something toward a target.

components.note: 哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'
哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ gēge bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
example.english: My older brother is three years older than me.
example.fact: Chinese kinship terms mark birth order where English just says “brother” — 哥哥 is strictly an older brother, and a younger one is 弟弟, a distinction with no single-word English equivalent.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.pinyin: Tā míngtiān yào zuò shǒushù.
example.english: He's having surgery tomorrow.
example.fact: The verb that pairs with 手术 is the generic 做 (“to do”) — 做手术 (“to do/perform/undergo surgery”) covers both the surgeon performing the operation and the patient undergoing it, with context alone telling the two roles apart.

components.note: 女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.pinyin: Méiyǒu bìyào zhème dānxīn.
example.english: There's no need to worry so much.
example.fact: 必要 (“necessary, a necessity,” used with 有/没有) is often confused with the similar-sounding 必须 (“must,” an adverb placed directly before a verb) — 有必要 (“it is necessary”) and 必须做 (“must do”) reveal the underlying grammatical split between the two.

components.note: 身 depicts a person's torso, originally showing a pregnant woman's body — later broadened to mean 'the body' in general.
辶 (walking/movement) — links 边's meaning to a boundary or edge one moves along.
臱 (biān) gives the sound — 边 is also pronounced biān, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí péi zài wǒ shēnbiān.
example.english: She has always stayed by my side.
example.fact: 身边 is literally “body-side” (身 “body” + 边 “side, edge”) — attaching a possessive pronoun before it (我身边, 你身边) is the standard Chinese way to say “near me / near you,” where English instead reaches for a preposition like “beside” or “near.”

components.note: 亻 (person) — 任 relates to a person taking on a responsibility or role.
壬 (rén) gives a hint of the sound — 任 is pronounced rèn, a connection that has shifted somewhat.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 任何人都可以参加这个比赛。
example.pinyin: Rènhérén dōu kěyǐ cānjiā zhège bǐsài.
example.english: Anyone can participate in this competition.
example.fact: 任何 (“any, whatever”) almost always pairs with 都 right after its noun (任何人都..., “anyone/everyone without exception...”) — 都 here doesn't mean “also” but reinforces totality, the same reinforcing job it does when question words turn into “any-” words, as in 谁都 or 什么都.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撒 describes scattering something by hand.
散 (to scatter, to disperse) — combined with the hand 扌, it gave 撒 its meaning 'to scatter, to release.'
讠 (speech) — 谎 describes false speech, a lie.
荒 (huāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 谎, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā cónglái bù sāhuǎng.
example.english: He never tells lies.
example.fact: 撒谎 is literally “to scatter a lie” (撒 “to scatter, cast” + 谎 “lie, falsehood”) — the same 撒 appears in 撒盐 (“to sprinkle salt”) and 撒网 (“to cast a net”), all built on the image of throwing something loosely outward.

components.note: 弋 (a dagger-axe/weapon) — represents military force.
止 (foot/to stop) — stopping an enemy by force of arms gave 武 its meaning 'military, martial.'
口 (a vessel), shown four times — a set of cooking vessels.
犬 (a dog) — guarding the vessels, the source of 器's meaning 'vessel, tool, instrument.'

example.hanzi: 警察在他家发现了武器。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zài tā jiā fāxiàn le wǔqì.
example.english: The police found weapons at his home.
example.fact: 武器 is literally “martial tool” (武 “military, martial” + 器 “vessel, tool, instrument”) — the same productive 器 gives 乐器 (“musical instrument”) and 电器 (“electrical appliance”), a recurring suffix for “tool/device of X kind.”

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痛 relates to physical pain or illness
甬 (yǒng) gives a sound distantly related to 痛's reading tòng, having drifted apart over time
艹 (grass/plant) — 苦 relates to the bitter taste of certain plants and herbs
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to 苦's reading kǔ

example.hanzi: 失去亲人的痛苦很难忘记。
example.pinyin: Shīqù qīnrén de tòngkǔ hěn nán wàngjì.
example.english: The pain of losing a loved one is hard to forget.
example.fact: 痛苦 doubles up two characters that are each already painful on their own — 痛 (“physical pain, ache”) and 苦 (“bitter, suffering”) — fusing a bodily sense with a tasting/emotional one into a single word that spans both physical and emotional suffering.

components.note: 入 (enter, put away) — 全 pictures something being placed into safekeeping.
玉 (jade) — a valuable treasure kept whole and undamaged, giving 全 its meaning of 'complete' or 'entire.'
阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē shū quánbù dōu shì wǒ de.
example.english: All of these books are mine.
example.fact: 全部 behaves as a noun for “the whole, the entirety” and often takes 都 afterward for emphasis (全部都...) — unlike 所有, which sits directly in front of a noun (所有的书, “all the books”), 全部 more often stands alone or trails the noun it refers back to.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ shǒujī fàng zài bāo lǐ le.
example.english: I put my phone in my bag.
example.fact: 手机 is literally “hand machine” (手 “hand” + 机 “machine”) — a plainly descriptive coinage for the mobile phone, the same instinct behind English “cell phone” and “mobile phone” rather than a borrowed or invented term.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 忘 relates to something slipping from the mind.
亡 (wáng) gives a sound distantly related to wàng, having drifted apart over time.
讠 (speech/writing) — the act of putting words down.
己 (oneself, private) — writing down one's own private notes or memories, giving 记 its meaning 'to record, remember.'

example.pinyin: Bié wàngjì dài sǎn.
example.english: Don't forget to bring an umbrella.
example.fact: 忘记 fuses 忘 (“to forget”) with its near-opposite 记 (“to remember, record”) into a single word meaning “to forget” — Chinese has a handful of compounds built the same way from an antonym pair, the best-known being 呼吸 (“to breathe,” from 呼 “to exhale” + 吸 “to inhale”).

components.note: 子 (child/seed) — 存's meaning 'to exist, survive' has been linked to a seed persisting to grow.
才 (cái) gives a sound hint — 存 is pronounced cún, sharing the initial consonant though the vowel and tone differ.
土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí yìzhí cúnzài.
example.english: This problem has always existed.
example.fact: 存在 combines 存 (“to survive, preserve”) and 在 (“to be present, at”), two characters that can each independently gesture at “existing” — reinforcing two near-synonyms into one word is the same strategy behind common words like 喜欢 (“to like,” from “joy” + “joy”) and 应该 (“should,” from two words each meaning roughly “ought to”).

components.note: 自 here depicts a head (the character also independently means 'nose, self').
丷 depicts hair atop the head — 首 originally pictured a head with hair, giving its meaning 'head, chief, first.'
止 (a foot, stepping forward) — 先 pictures someone moving ahead of another.
儿 (a person) — one person stepping ahead of another gave 先 its meaning 'before' or 'first.'

example.hanzi: 首先,我要感谢大家的支持。
example.pinyin: Shǒuxiān, wǒ yào gǎnxiè dàjiā de zhīchí.
example.english: First of all, I want to thank everyone for their support.
example.fact: 首先 is a formal opener for listing points (首先...然后...最后..., “first...then...finally...”) fitting written or public-speaking contexts — in casual conversation, speakers often just say plain 先 instead, saving 首先 for more structured moments.

example.hanzi: 会议邀请了老师、学生以及家长。
example.pinyin: Huìyì yāoqǐng le lǎoshī, xuésheng yǐjí jiāzhǎng.
example.english: The meeting invited teachers, students, as well as parents.
example.fact: 以及 is generally reserved for the last, often somewhat distinct item in a list, especially in formal writing, while 和 or 跟 handle everyday “and” between ordinary items — reaching for 以及 signals a small shift in kind or importance for what follows.

components.note: 丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ gèrén de kànfǎ.
example.english: This is my personal opinion.
example.fact: 个人 sits directly in front of a noun to mean “personal, individual” (个人看法, 个人信息) without any adjective-forming suffix the way English needs “-al” to turn “person” into “personal” — the noun itself does double duty.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 代 relates to a person's place in time.
弋 (a stake used to mark or catch something) — combined with 亻 (person), 代 came to mean a 'generation' or 'era,' and 'to take the place of' someone.
毛 (fur, hair) — 表 originally pictured a fur garment worn on the outside.
衣 (clothing) — an outer fur wrap gave 表 its meaning of 'outer' or 'surface,' and later, 'to express' (showing something on the surface).

example.hanzi: 他代表公司参加了会议。
example.pinyin: Tā dàibiǎo gōngsī cānjiā le huìyì.
example.english: He represented the company at the meeting.
example.fact: 代表 splits cleanly along its two characters' older senses: 代 (“to take the place of, substitute”) and 表 (“to express, show”) — together, roughly “to stand in for and express on behalf of,” a fairly transparent path to the modern meanings “to represent” and “representative.”

components.note: 扌 (hand) — relates directly to 持's meaning 'to hold, maintain.'
寺 (sì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from chí.

example.hanzi: 只要坚持下去,你就会成功。
example.pinyin: Zhǐyào jiānchí xiàqù, nǐ jiù huì chénggōng.
example.english: As long as you keep persisting, you will succeed.
example.fact: 坚持 very often takes the directional complement 下去 (“to continue on,” literally “go down”) right after it — 坚持下去 (“to keep persisting”) is one of the most common fixed collocations built around this word.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
⺷ (sheep, related to 羊) — 义 relates to what is right or moral, linked to the idea of sacrificial sheep used in rituals of righteousness.
乂 (yì) gives the sound — 义 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这次旅行对我很有意义。
example.pinyin: Zhècì lǚxíng duì wǒ hěn yǒu yìyì.
example.english: This trip was very meaningful to me.
example.fact: 意义 is almost always framed with 有 for “meaningful” (有意义) and 没有 for “meaningless” (没有意义) — since the word itself is a noun, Chinese needs this 有/没有 wrapper to do the job English gets straight from the adjective “meaningful.”

components.note: 承 depicts multiple hands supporting and lifting something from below — giving 承 its meaning 'to support, to receive, to inherit.'
讠 (speech) — 认 relates to recognizing or acknowledging something, often expressed through words.
人 (rén) gives the sound — 认 is pronounced rèn, a close variant of the same sound.

example.hanzi: 他终于承认了自己的错误。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú chéngrèn le zìjǐ de cuòwù.
example.english: He finally admitted his mistake.
example.fact: 承认 covers both “to admit” (a fault) and “to recognize” (a government, a diploma, a fact) in diplomatic and legal registers, as in 承认一个国家 (“to recognize a country”) — one word spanning what English splits into “admit” and “recognize.”

components.note: 折 (to break) here suggests something that must never be broken.
言 (speech) sits below — words that must not be broken, giving 誓 its meaning 'oath, vow.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiàng nǐ fāshì, zhè shì zhēn de.
example.english: I swear to you, this is true.
example.fact: 发誓 is literally “to issue an oath” (发 “to issue, send out” + 誓 “oath, vow”) — the same productive 发 turns up in 发言 (“to speak up”) and 发信 (“to send a letter”), all sharing the sense of something being released or put forth.

components.note: 王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.
由 resembles 田 (a field) with a stem or road extending from it — pointing the way toward a source, which gave 由 its meaning of 'from' or 'cause.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ méiyǒu lǐyóu shēngqì.
example.english: You have no reason to be angry.
example.fact: 理由 and 原因 both translate as “reason,” but 理由 leans toward a justification someone offers for a choice, while 原因 leans toward the objective cause of an event — 没有理由 (“no justification”) reads differently from 没有原因 (“no cause”).

components.note: 日 (sun) — 显 relates to something bright and clearly visible in the light
业 (yè) gives a loose sound connection to 显's reading xiǎn
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Xiǎnrán, tā méiyǒu zuò hǎo zhǔnbèi.
example.english: Clearly, he wasn't well prepared.
example.fact: 显然 typically opens a sentence as a stand-alone adverb commenting on the whole clause that follows, much like English “clearly” or “obviously” at a sentence's start — a common marker for a speaker's confident inference, in both writing and speech.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick, action) — 政 relates to administering or governing.
正 (zhèng) gives the sound — 政 is also pronounced zhèng, an exact match.
广 (a wide shelter/roof) — relates to 府's meaning 'government office, mansion,' a large official building.
付 (fù) gives a sound hint — 府 is pronounced fǔ, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ xuānbù le xīn de zhèngcè.
example.english: The government announced a new policy.
example.fact: 政府 combines 政 (“governance, politics”) with 府 (“official residence, mansion”) — 府 alone also names a seat of administration in words like 首府 (“provincial capital”), reflecting an older habit of naming a ruling body after the building that housed it.

components.note: 冫 (originally a mark for repetition, unrelated to its later meaning 'ice') — suggests something done more than once.
欠 (a person yawning, mouth open) — repeated yawning gave 次 its meaning of a 'time' or occurrence, as in counting how many times something happens.

example.pinyin: Zhècì kǎoshì hěn nán.
example.english: This exam was very difficult.
example.fact: 次 is Mandarin's general measure word for counting discrete occurrences (一次, 两次, 这次) — the counterpart to 个 as the default measure word for objects, which makes 这次 (“this occurrence, this time”) the event-counting twin of 这个 (“this one”).

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.hanzi: 他在这里做生意已经十年了。
example.pinyin: Tā zài zhèlǐ zuò shēngyi yǐjīng shí nián le.
example.english: He has been doing business here for ten years.
example.fact: 生意 has two separate CEDICT entries sharing the same characters but differing in tone: everyday shēngyi, with a neutral second syllable, means “business, trade” and explains this word's high frequency, while the fully-toned shēngyì is a rarer, more literary word for “life force, vitality” — the same characters, a different register and reading entirely.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — encountering someone often happens while moving or traveling.
禺 (yú) gives a sound close to yù, with the tone shifted.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我在路上遇到了一个老朋友。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài lùshang yùdào le yí gè lǎo péngyou.
example.english: I ran into an old friend on the road.
example.fact: 遇到 pairs 遇 (“to encounter”) with the same success-marking 到 also seen in 做到 (rank 452 in this batch) and the common verb 看到 (“to see, to succeed in seeing”) — the compound stresses that the encounter actually happened, rather than merely being attempted or hoped for.

components.note: 卩 (a kneeling figure) — a hungry person kneeling down, about to eat.
皀 (a bowl of food) — the meal in front of them, giving 即 its sense of imminent action, 'right away, that is to say.'
亻 (person) — 使 involves a person carrying out a task.
吏 (a government official) — 使 originally referred to an official sent to carry out orders, giving rise to the meaning 'to make someone do something' or 'to use.'

example.pinyin: Jíshǐ xiàyǔ, wǒmen yě huì qù.
example.english: Even if it rains, we'll still go.
example.fact: 即使 is almost always paired with 也 in the clause that follows (即使...,也...), the same two-part frame that 虽然 forms with 但是 — Chinese marks both halves of the sentence where English's single “even if” only needs to appear once.

components.note: 讠 (speech/writing) — the act of putting words down.
己 (oneself, private) — writing down one's own private notes or memories, giving 记 its meaning 'to record, remember.'
亻 (person) — the one settling somewhere.
主 (host, master) — the idea of a person settled in a place as if hosting it, giving 住 its meaning 'to live, reside, stay.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng jìzhu wǒ de míngzi.
example.english: Please remember my name.
example.fact: 记住 pairs 记 (“to record, remember”) with the resultative complement 住 (“to hold firmly, to stay”) — 住 here doesn't mean “to live” but marks that the remembering “sticks,” the same job it does in 抓住 (“to grab hold of”) and 站住 (“to stand firm”).

components.note: 至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào
夂 (a foot, to go) — 处 relates to arriving somewhere.
卜 (a mark or flag) — planting a marker after arriving gave 处 its meaning of 'a place' or 'to settle, deal with.'

example.pinyin: Tā dàochù zhǎo tā de qiánbāo.
example.english: He looked everywhere for his wallet.
example.fact: 到处 is literally “to every place” (到 “to reach, arrive” + 处 “place, location”) and works as an adverb sitting directly before the verb it modifies (到处找, “to search everywhere”), unlike English “everywhere,” which can also trail after the verb or a preposition.

components.note: The upper part, related to 土, traditionally depicted one person's fate.
干 depicted a contrasting fate — the character set two outcomes side by side, with the fortunate one giving 幸 its meaning 'lucky, fortunate.'
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 运's meaning 'to move, transport,' and by extension 'fortune,' the movement of one's life.
云 (yún) gives a sound hint — 运 is pronounced yùn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zìjǐ hěn xìngyùn.
example.english: I feel very lucky.
example.fact: 幸运 works as both an adjective (“lucky”) and a noun (“good fortune, luck”), so 很幸运 (“very lucky”) and 是我的幸运 (“is my good fortune”) both use the same word unchanged — another case in this list of a word crossing freely between adjective and noun.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.pinyin: Nàshí wǒmen hái hěn niánqīng.
example.english: At that time, we were still very young.
example.fact: 那时 pairs the far demonstrative 那 (“that”) with 时 (“time”), mirroring how 这时 (“at this time, right now”) is built — the same far/near split behind 那个/这个 and 那么/这么 carries over consistently into this pair as well.

components.note: A pictograph of an ancient forked weapon, such as a club or shield-tipped spear — the tool image later extended to 干's meanings 'to do, to work' and, in another reading, 'dry.'
亻 (person) — 什 originally referred to a group of people.
十 (ten) — combined with 亻 (person), 什 originally described a group of ten; the character later came to be used for the common word 什么 (what).

example.pinyin: Nǐ zài zhèr gànshénme?
example.english: What are you doing here?
example.fact: 干什么 is the blunter, more colloquial cousin of 做什么 — 干 as a verb for “to do” carries a rougher, more casual edge than the neutral 做, so depending on tone of voice 干什么 can land as impatient or accusatory in a way the flat English translation “what are you doing” doesn't capture.

meanings: matter that needs to be settled

components.note: 儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.pinyin: Nǐ jīntiān yǒu shìr ma?
example.english: Do you have something on today?
example.fact: The 儿 in 事儿 is a Beijing-rooted retroflex ending (erhua) that fuses into the previous syllable's pronunciation rather than forming its own syllable — 事儿 is pronounced as one syllable, “shir,” not two.

components.note: 犭 (dog) — 犯 originally related to a dog attacking, later extended to any act of violation
㔾 (jié) gives a sound distantly related to 犯's reading fàn, having drifted apart over time
罒 (a net) — the law closing in around wrongdoing
非 (wrong) — the wrongdoing itself, caught in the net

example.hanzi: 他因为犯罪被送进了监狱。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi fànzuì bèi sòng jìn le jiānyù.
example.english: He was sent to prison because he committed a crime.
example.fact: 犯罪 combines 犯 (“to violate, offend”) with 罪 (“crime, sin”) — the same productive 犯 shows up in 犯错 (“to make a mistake”) and 犯法 (“to break the law”), a recurring verb for “to commit/violate” across different kinds of wrongdoing.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跳 describes an action done with the feet, jumping.
兆 (zhào) gives a rhyme close to tiào, with the initial and tone shifted.
無-shaped top pictures a dancer holding decorated sleeves or fans.
舛 below pictures a pair of feet, together giving 舞 its meaning 'to dance.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhōumò jīngcháng qù tiàowǔ.
example.english: We often go dancing on weekends.
example.fact: 跳舞 is a verb-object compound, literally “to jump a dance” (跳 “to jump, leap” + 舞 “dance”) — like other activity verbs of this shape, such as 唱歌 (“to sing a song”) and 游泳 (“to swim a swim”), the “object” half can even be separated out (跳了一支舞, “danced a dance”) despite 跳舞 feeling like one fused verb.
